subtopic: SPRINGHILL, N.S.-REQUEST FOR PROVISION OF WORKS PROJECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that question was asked as well by the Leader of the Opposition. I received a telegram from Mr. A. J. Mason, chairman of the citizens' industrial committee of Springhill, Nova Scotia, much along the lines of the suggestions that have been made in whole or in part by the hon. member for Cumberland earlier.
At the time I received this telegram referring to the special measures that were being taken by the federal government in the Cape Breton area to assist in providing jobs for the coal miners affected by the mine closures, a request was made that a similar program be introduced at Springhill because of the mine closures in that area and the fact that some of the miners were unemployed. The house will recall that the closing of the Springhill mines occurred several years ago, and at that time special measures of various kinds were taken, including assistance to coal miners in finding employment elsewhere.

On June 23 I made the following reply to Mr. Mason:
Your telegram of recent date has been receiving attention. As you know a new penitentiary has been established and a new mine opened at Spring-hill recently. In addition the Springhill area has this month been designated by order in council as a surplus manpower area in which double depreciation will be allowed for income tax purposes to new industries. Any further measures that may be taken from time to time by the government of Canada will be announced.
I received a further telegram from Mr. Mason on July 3 repeating the request of the earlier telegram and asking that the federal government provide assistance in the construction of a new hospital and a vocational training school, and for the establishment of a national park in the area. Furthermore, it was also requested that the Canadian National Railways take over from Dosco the spur line between Springhill and Springhill Junction.
Apart from the special measures of assistance mentioned in my telegram to Mr. Mason, the Department of National Health and Welfare has approved a hospital grant in the amount of $178,360 to the All Saints' hospital corporation. The question as to whether a vocational training school should be built in the Springhill area is a matter for the provincial government in the first instance, although, as the house knows, special legislation passed during this session is applicable to suitable vocational training schools anywhere in Canada.
As to the railway spur line, it is being studied by the Department of Transport, the Canadian National Railways and the government of Nova Scotia. I should add further that my colleague the Minister of Public Works recently announced plans for the construction of a new federal building at Springhill.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO THE REGULATIONS RESPECTING SHIPBUILDING SUBSIDIES
speechtext:
As hon. members will recall, I announced in the house on May 12 a new policy respecting government assistance to Canadian ship operators and shipyards. I also stated that the methods of determining approved costs for this purpose and other particulars relating to administration of this plan will be prescribed by regulations approved by the governor in council. We are making good progress in the drafting of these regulations, and I hope they will be ready in the near future.
However, in order to avoid delay in proceeding with projects in shipyards on the part of potential large purchasers, we have introduced an interim procedure by which prospective purchaser and shipyard jointly can write in to seek assurance in principle that the project they have in mind would be covered by the subsidy policy. Accordingly a provisional application for ship construction assistance has been prepared for the use of those who may wish to proceed with the formulation of an application at this time. This application form has already been given to the following associations: Canadian Shipbuilding and Ship Repairing Association;

Inquiries of the Ministry Canadian Shipowners Association; Dominion Marine Association; B.C. Towboat Owners' Association.
In writing to them in this connection I advised that respective applicants should be guided by the following general considerations:
1.	The approved cost of vessel construction would be the price at which a contract is placed as a result of competitive tenders. Where a contract is not placed with the lowest bidder, or where there is only one tender received, or where a contract is placed without the calling of tenders, the government might, after investigation, fix a lower figure as being the approved cost. In all cases a firm figure would be established upon approval of an application which would not be subject to escalation and would be payable to the shipyard in the customary form of progress payments.
2.	The proposed construction is to incorporate the maximum Canadian content that is practicable and consistent with availability and economy. If less than such maximum Canadian content is proposed, then the approved cost of construction may be reduced by such amount as the government may deem appropriate.
3.	The owner for whom the vessel is to be built must be Canadian, whether a person, partnership, corporation or provincial or municipal government, or agency of such a government. Such owner would be required to undertake to maintain the vessel on Canadian registry for at least ten years. Any disposal of the vessel during that period would be subject to appropriate governmental approval.
4.	The prospective owner and builder would be required to make joint application for the subsidy in accordance with the form "Provisional Application for Ship Construction Assistance", or such other form as may be prescribed.
5.	The applicants would be required to establish their respective financial responsibility to the satisfaction of the government. This would normally include a requirement to carry insurance to protect the government against bankruptcy of either applicant and to cover builders risk and such other contingencies as may be specified.
6.	Where a vessel is disposed of by a taxpayer and the proceeds or any part of the proceeds are used to finance or to assist in financing construction which is eligible for subsidy, such use would not qualify the taxpayer for the benefits set out in section 4 of the Canadian Vessel Construction Assistance Act, i.e. the portion of the proceeds so used would be subject to recapture of any excess depreciation that has been claimed.

7.	Other provisions affecting shipping and shipbuilding are being reviewed, including legislative provisions, and changes may be announced or recommended to parliament in due course, but the government does not propose any material change in those sections of the Canadian Vessel Construction Assistance Act which allow an accelerated rate of depreciation on the owner's net investment or which authorize the claiming of reserves for special surveys.
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to say that already ship owners and shipbuilders have signed contracts on the basis of the foregoing prescription.

subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, July 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fleming (EgUnton) for the third reading of Bill No. C-114, respecting the Bank of Canada.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what I have said so far during the course of the debate was designed to show that the views expressed by the opposition regarding their affection for the bill of rights was but lip service to principles which they had disavowed so frequently and so wantonly during their period of office. What I am going to do today is cover in general some of the matters that have not been dealt with in extenso as yet.
At the same time I am able to say that the publication of a letter yesterday by Mr. Coyne, to which he attached various letters which have passed between him and the Minister of Finance, will in very considerable measure reduce the length of my remarks, for they themselves constitute an answer to many of the matters that have been raised by the opposition. Indeed they are a revelation of what the Minister of Finance had stated to be the fact, that there was a vast division of opinion between the views of the government and the views of the governor.
I think I should also say that the Bank of Canada Act contains schedule A-to which I will do nothing more than make the casual reference necessary to place it on Hansard- which is the oath of fidelity and secrecy. It reads as follows:
I,-do solemnly swear that I will faithfully, truly and to the best of my judgment, skill and ability, execute and perform the duties required of me as a director (officer or employee as the case may be) of the Bank of Canada and which properly relate to any office or position in the said bank held by me.
I further solemnly swear that I will not communicate or allow to be communicated to any person not legally entitled thereto any information relating to the affairs of the bank, nor will I allow any such person to inspect or have access to any books or documents belonging to or in the possession of the bank and relating to the business of the bank.
Sir, I am not going to enter into recriminations. I am not going to answer in kind. I have found myself to be subject of bitter personal attacks far and beyond the realm of criticism ordinarily accepted and necessary for our parliamentary system. I have never answered personal attacks. I do not intend to start on this occasion. I do say, however, that whatever feelings of some Canadians may have been at the beginning of this debate, the last two epistles sent out from the ivory tower, irresponsible and intemperate, sent out on the letterheads and in envelopes belonging to the Bank of Canada and delivered by a personal messenger of the bank, make one wonder.

subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext:
Sir, these letters reveal an attitude which, if accepted by the government, would result in two sovereignties in 90205-6-485
Governor of Bank of Canada Canada, the government of Canada and the governor of the Bank of Canada; but not in that order. They would set up a rival government. They have established beyond any question that the views of the governor and the policies of this government as revealed prior to and in the budget are incompatible. They have revealed, too, that the attitude of the governor and responsible government and its maintenance are not compatible. He has shown that there are irreconcilable differences on basic policies. Throughout the correspondence he has gone beyond the field of monetary policy and has declared himself in direct conflict with government policies on fiscal, financial and commercial matters.
To listen to the official opposition today one would think that was a recent attitude on his part. I would ask hon. members opposite to read Hansard of August 10, 1956, page 7351. In view of the announcement last night by the Bank of Canada that its interest rate has been raised to the unprecedented high level of 31 per cent, will the minister advise the house what is the purpose behind this new move on the part of the Bank of Canada?

The ground rules of the Bank of Canada, as it were, were set out in the report of the royal commission on banking and currency in 1933 at page 63:
A central bank is at the same time an instrument and a force. As an instrument it is the means by which the state, which must necessarily retain ultimate sovereignty in matters respecting the currency, can give effect to the national policy.
That is the principle on which it was set up, and in volume 1 of the proceedings of the commission, at page 92, there is the evidence of Professor W. A. Carrothers, of Vancouver, as follows:
No one suggests that this board (that is, the bank) should become the governmental authority of Canada, but it should become the instrument through which a truly national policy can be carried out in such a federation as we have in Canada today ... Naturally, it would have to work in co-operation with the many policies of the country. You cannot have one institution working one way and another institution working another.

"I think it is always of interest to know what are the principles which should actuate a public servant." New tax laws, new amendments to the Criminal Code, as well as other acts of parliament may and do from time to time operate to modify or affect rights of persons; but it is never said and it cannot be said that a person is not bound by such laws or such statutes unless he is given an opportunity to come before parliament.
This idea is based on the distinction between the functions of parliament and the functions of the courts. These functions are different. The legislative function is concerned with the making of laws, a function which can be performed only by parliament or by bodies to which parliament has delegated authority. The judicial authority is performed by the courts and other tribunals established in accordance with laws passed by parliament.

When Mr. Coyne was appointed governor it was for the purpose of providing an efficient operation within the ambit of the Bank of Canada Act. The duty and right of parliament is to act when any responsibilities undertaken are not carried out; and it is obvious that they have not been carried out. One just has to read those letters. relationship of the central bank to the government of this country. All that could have been avoided if the government had taken, what the Prime Minister at long last acknowledged this morning, the proper course in the event of a dispute between the governor of the Bank of Canada and the government, not only in the field of monetary policy but in matters that touch fiscal, debt management and financial policy as well.
I say now that in view of the disclosures made yesterday by the governor of the Bank of Canada-and I am not now seeking to defend the method by which those disclosures were made-one would have expected the Prime Minister of this country, not to have to be asked to agree to the setting up of a committee for the purpose of examining this matter, but to have joined with the rest of us, in giving this house the lead, in demanding that an examination be made in a committee of this house of the disclosures, and particularly those mentioned by Mr. Coyne yesterday. No, Mr. Speaker, there was not any mention at all of the substance of the governor's statement of yesterday and of the three letters which accompanied that statement and which were made available to the public.
The Prime Minister has asked why all this fuss by the opposition at this time when the usefulness of the governor has ceased. He suggested that was what members of the Liberal opposition had affirmed. I say to the Prime Minister that the governor's usefulness now may have ceased, but we contend that his rights as an individual in Canada have not ceased.
We are not arguing, as the Prime Minister sought to suggest in the introduction of a red herring, that the supremacy of parliament is involved. No one questions the right of parliament, under section 91 of the British North America Act, to exercise whatever power, whatever act, whatever judgment, whatever disposition it wishes to make. Of course parliament is supreme, supreme over every emanation of the crown, supreme over the governor of the Bank of Canada. Parliament's word is final. There is no dispute about that.
The issue is a simple one. It is simply whether or not in a matter so complicated as this, where statements made by the Prime Minister are so diametrically opposed to those of the governor of the Bank of Canada, we are going to have a proper determination of that issue, not by the vote of a strong majority, but by the vote of a committee which conscientiously and objectively wishes to examine all of the facts.
We have based our contention upon the inalienable right that has been recognized in

this country and in all countries of the commonwealth, as well as in most countries of the western world, now for many centuries, and which has now been confirmed in the bill of rights introduced by the Prime Minister on July 1, 1960. The Prime Minister says that the bill of rights does not apply to non judicial processes. I have before me a copy of the bill of rights which bears the signature of the Prime Minister and a quotation from one of his speeches. This is the printed copy which is distributed throughout the country for the price of $1. This statement will be found in the copy of the bill of rights. It says nothing about judicial process; it says nothing about being confined to matters involving criminal law. It says:
No law of Canada shall be construed or applied so as to (e) deprive a person-
And the governor of the Bank of Canada is a person.
-of the right to a fair hearing in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice for the determination of his rights and obligations.
Are we to say that the bill of rights, this document which I hold in my hand, is something which applies only to those, as I said the other day, who are charged with a violation of the criminal law? If that is so, what we are saying then is that the bill of rights applies only to those who are charged with crimes, but it does not apply to those who are in the eyes of society guilty of something less than a crime; it does not apply to one who has served his country, as has the governor of the bank. Perhaps we will not all agree with his policies. We do not, but nevertheless he stands as a citizen honourable and fearless in the position that he takes. Are we to take the position that the bill of rights applies to a criminal and not to one of our top officials, namely the governor of the Bank of Canada? Are we to say that in this country, this free country, with our bill of rights? Are we to say with regard to the governor of the Bank of Canada that we cannot accord him the kind of treatment that is applied to other individuals in other countries? If he did receive that letter, then the information that he gave this house when we were about to take a vote was not in harmony with the facts. It was not a statement made in accord with the truth. So we have this situation. The governor of the Bank of Canada has successfully indicated that there was not only one meeting but that there were four meetings at which the deputy minister and others were present. He
Governor of Bank of Canada has further contradicted the Minister of Finance who said that there was no communication between himself and the governor of the bank. He has successfully established, from the action of the presidents of the banks themselves and from section 71 of the Bank Act, that the decision with regard to the percentage of liquidity asset reserves of the chartered banks was a decision which arose not out of any power residing in the governor under the Bank of Canada Act but as a result of a decision voluntarily entered into by the chartered banks themselves, first in 1955, and then continued on into subsequent years.
Then we have the further contradiction of the statement of the Minister of Finance by the governor who pointed out that the governor had offered to go before a committee of this house.
Are we not now faced with an unfinished situation, Mr. Speaker: The matter was not concluded with the final observations of the speech of the Minister of Finance the other day because since that time, as I say, we have further material before us, and it is material that takes serious issue in points of substance involving the credibility of two Canadian citizens, one the governor of the bank and the other the Minister of Finance. Are we now to take the position that this matter is over? Are we to take the position that this house is going to resolve this matter finally and send it to another place without having taken into account the circumstances involved in the further disclosures that have been made by the governor of the Bank of Canada?
I regret to say, Mr. Speaker, that in view of the information given the committee of the whole by the minister on July 4 and 5, information which has clearly been shown to be inaccurate, misleading and untrue, there is no course open now to the Minister of Finance under our system of government, if we want to live up to the traditions of the parliament in the United Kingdom, other than to turn in his seals of office.

To take any other course will be to leave this house, a year after the bill of rights was passed, saying that we were proud on July 1, 1960 to pass this measure confirming, as it does, the basic freedoms and human rights accorded to all Canadians. While we were proud to place this measure on our statute books, we regret that the government of the country, a government with a great majority behind it, was not prepared to take a step consistent with the implications of that bill of rights and afford the fullest hearing in this matter, thereby giving one individual the right -and giving the Minister of Finance the right -of having his side of the case properly exposed for final judgment before we pass this measure in final form on third reading.

The real issue does not even concern Mr. Coyne but concerns what will be the relationship between the Bank of Canada and the Minister of Finance of this government. We have reached a point now where we cannot get the information in this house but must go to our mailboxes every day in order to find out what is going on. I suggest we can only deal with the relationship of the Bank of Canada to this parliament with knowledge which can be gained solely by questioning in a committee of this house. That is the only means by which we can gain knowledge which will allow us to come to a sensible conclusion. The issue is not a question of the supremacy of parliament, but one of the intelligent conduct of parliament. Perhaps Mr. Coyne as the governor of the Bank of Canada is not covered by the bill of rights, but Mr. Coyne as a man


should be heard because he is a citizen of this nation, and the bill of rights applies to him as a citizen.

For four years we have had indecision and lack of co-operation during which the Minister of Finance refused to set his own house in order, with the obvious resulting disorder.
I am sure the people of this nation are going to wonder to what extent policy at the top has meant suffering at the bottom. We have had the highest unemployment rate in the western world this past winter. Families have been suffering and we are led to ask to what extent this has occurred because of chaos and confusion in this government, and its incompetence in putting its own house in order. Mr. Speaker, when the Prime Minister was speaking this morning I was interested in trying to catch in a personal way the thrill and the reaction in the public galleries and in the house to what was said. There is no question about it: He made the kind of speech that impresses people and moves them along a certain line with him, persuading his listeners that somehow this parliament had a case and that somehow the governor of the Bank of Canada had got in the way and was impeding the whole role of the elected representatives as reflected in this parliament. I wish to enter one caveat or reservation and say this from the point of view of an individual member.
I think it can be put in this form. There is a great deal of misunderstanding or, if you wish, nonsense talked about the responsibility of parliament and the supremacy of parliament. What is supreme in this particular parliament or in any Canadian parliament? Is it the Prime Minister? It seems to be that this is what it is; that the Prime Minister as the peak figure in the executive that is marshalled in this House of Commons feels that he is supreme in a sense and the rest of us, those of us who may not disagree, really cannot have or should not have in this forum, if he disagrees, the opportunity of finding out what parliament really means. It seems to me that what parliament really means is that each one of us has the right to examine and hear someone who is in power and carrying out his job as a result of the pleasure of this parliament.
I and many of my colleagues have felt on election night when the final totals are computed, that an incredible amount of power immediately falls upon the shoulders of the Prime Minister. I thought, in the campaign fought in the previous two elections, that the government were cognizant of this as a result of the stand they took in the debates in 1955 and 1956 but apparently they have very quickly taken over the conception of the supremacy of parliament which means the supremacy of the Prime Minister. This is one side of the Coyne-Fleming controversy. It seems to me we need some political thought and some political theory with relation to whether parliament as such, including all of

Governor of Bank of Canada us, is a legal fiction or not, or whether parliament really means the supreme power, not of all of us but of the Prime Minister.
The other aspect of the Coyne controversy, Mr. Speaker, that is most intriguing, is the comic opera aspect of it. When I think what a small place Ottawa is, when I think that the Minister of Finance has an office just across the street from the governor of the Bank of Canada-with a strong throw you could easily pitch a rock over-when I think of the social milieu and the milieu of the officials and executives in Ottawa is not a tremendously great one; we are not like New York and Washington where hundreds of people are surging in all directions. These people are constantly meeting and bumping into each other, both in the executive and in the public service side of Ottawa. How we could have a situation going on as it is now revealed through the correspondence is nothing but comic opera. The Minister of Finance who really does not care for the governor of the Bank of Canada does not really do anything about getting rid of him until he is almost clear of him just through passage of time. This seems to me almost incredible. After 34 years, almost four, in this small world of Ottawa, where all these clashes are taking place below the surface the Minister of Finance never got together with the governor of the Bank of Canada and worked out either some rapport or some rapprochement between them or worked out some way of having his say in so far as monetary and fiscal policy is concerned.
I think there is confusion on the part of all of us with respect to this issue, and unlike some of the speakers on both sides of the house I do not know that the Canadian people have much of a clue as to what is involved in this issue. I think they are tremendously confused by it all. I do not think they are able to conceive of the confusion that must exist in a government that for 3J years will put up with a public servant who is going around the country talking on issues that quite obviously affect public and government policy. To wind up after all that with this kind of hassle involving letters being posted and confidences being broken in public means that the situation is simply a ridiculous one.
The only thing I can suggest as an individual and on behalf of our party is that perhaps the one way to get rid of the confusion, although for a time the situation may be made more confusing, is for the government to go to the people at once on this issue or on like issues that it feels are associated with it and we will get the matter


cleared up once and for all whether Canadians want to go on with a government that is so incompetent and so much given to procrastination.

Mr. Chairman, last evening when we began the discussion on this bill I pointed out that one of our major concerns still remained unsolved and that we were not alone in speaking of this problem. Most of the associations are in agreement with us that there are two main reasons for changing the Civil Service Act. The first is that the act should be brought up to date and the wording changed so that the changes which have taken place over the years since 1919 in departments, in the organization of government and in the relationship of civil servants may be incorporated in the act.
It should be pointed out that in 1919 approximately 70 per cent of the employees of the United Kingdom government were classed as civil servants. Today less than 41 per cent of government employees are civil service employees. These figures were taken from the experience of the mother parliament. I am not aware that any figures are available for our own civil service, but there is a similarity between the two situations. This has resulted in most of these associations asking for one civil service; that all employees of the government should be brought under the terms of the Civil Service Act. This would bring our civil service numbers into a much higher percentage ratio than is the case at the present time.
The second point worthy of consideration is the fact that although the bill has been amended several times it does not point out, and the government has failed to point out, what the arrangement will be for negotiation such as would allow the establishment of a much better contract for civil servants. In this connection I should point out that the committee was informed on a number of occasions that we should not look on Bill No. C-71 as an agreement covering civil servants in their relationships with the civil service commission and with the government, but that these conditions, which would be normally reserved for a collective bargaining agreement, would be contained for the most part in regulations which would apply to the operation of this measure.

Civil Service Act
I feel that this is not a desirable situation, because I believe that civil servants should know with whom they are negotiating. They should know how far they must go before they can learn what the decision is to be in relation to requests made to the government and what appeal is possible from that decision. My personal opinion is that the civil service should deal first through their pay bureau and through the relationship with the civil service commission. They should decide on the rates for a particular classification. Of course, in the initial stages the associations will make their submissions and the departmental heads will, I presume, make counter submissions. But the full submission will be carried to the treasury board by the commission itself. Once the commission has taken the proposals to the government, and by government I mean either the governor in council or the treasury board as representative of the government, the commission should, in my opinion, step out of the picture as having fulfilled its function. It is in this relation that I think we have to make some improvement if we are going to have a satisfactory method of continuing associations.
The requests that are made, when they are presented to the government, will have to be considered of necessity in the light of the financial structure and financial condition of the treasury and of the government, and any requests which come from the civil service will have to take into consideration the ability of the government to pay the increases in salaries which are requested. It is in this field that I think we should have an impartial tribunal, possibly on the same lines as the arbitration tribunals in England, which would be able to make a final arbitration between the employee and the employer, in this case the civil service associations and organizations and the government or the treasury branch on the other hand. I believe that this decision should be conclusive because I am of the opinion that a strike is unlikely and is probably going to be unduly costly if it takes place in the civil service as a method of reaching a final decision. We have been learning in the last few days that the decision of parliament is final in all instances, but I think that rather than go to parliament, which would probably, in some cases, involve an action of the kind we have just taken in another field, there should be a more orderly manner of handling the final appeal and negotiations.
The civil service association recently indicated its views on this bill. It made it known that the association and its members are disappointed that certain basic principles of their position could not gain acceptance

in the committee or from the government.
The association stated:
We are as concerned with too rigid legislation as is the government. However, we do not feel that the position we took before the committee requesting negotiation, consultation and arbitration implied any rigidity whatsoever. We viewed these principles as minimum safeguards to the rights of civil servants.
The statement went on:
Our major area of concern is the lack of definition of what constitutes consultation and whether it is synonymous with negotiation as we view it. We are also concerned that there is no means whatsoever in the legislation to solve fundamental points of disagreement which must, from time to time, arise regardless of how much good faith is evidenced by the parties concerned. We thus feel that the refusal of some constitutionally acceptable form of arbitration will inhibit the staff associations in their representations.
Our other major concern is the government's belief that after so many years we can in effect only now begin to evolve a satisfactory system of dealing between it and its employees on matters concerning salaries, wages and working conditions.
They go on to point out that they do not think we should not, as in the present bill, leave this matter to evolution and the development of something which may arise from evolution. They think we should decide how we are going to arrive at a proper method of handling the matter of negotiations. They think that this should be implied in the bill and a date set for revision, if revision is not possible at the present time.
Most organizations were concerned also with the delegation of authority. The bill, unlike the previous measures, gives to the deputy heads considerable authority which they did not have before, and arguments were put forward on both sides of the question. Some said this would result in a much faster method of handling problems arising in the department, that it would allow a much closer examination of problems than might be undertaken by an impartial body not familiar with the particular problems in the department. On the other hand it was argued that this would allow for the delegation of authority down through the department and that this would in most cases prohibit any appeal from decisions. It was felt that the commission itself, which would be delegating its authority, does not exercise as much influence through this bill as the Heeney report suggested it should, and that this, its worst feature, could mean a great increase in what has been considered to be departmental patronage-patronage which may take place because of the likes and dislikes and the close working relationship of people within a department. This, of course, has happened in the past under the act and I presume it will happen again. There are two or three very good examples. I do not wish to go into

these now. They have been brought to the attention of the commission and of the department concerned and they indicate that what I am saying is true and that some change is needed. This was a problem in England on a number of occasions. The act there was changed to make the type of operation which we are considering today a possibility for a number of years, and then it was decided to go back to the system of Whitley councils and eliminate some of the delegation of authority.
I was interested to learn that a number of members of this committee were interested in continuing to give more than lip service to veterans preference. This preference in my opinion has been abused over the years not because it is not believed in but because other factors have been given more consideration. Where two equal individuals apply for the same position the preference is to be given to the veteran. I hope this situation will continue in order that those individuals who have served in the armed forces will have some advantage.
I was very interested in the speech made last night by the hon. member for Hull regarding bilingual training. This country is bilingual by constitution and I suggest there is a decided advantage generally to the Canadian people as a result. I feel that if an opportunity were provided to civil servants to become bilingual through a government implemented training program we would gain a tremendous advantage. I suggest such a training program should be adopted by the federal government so that individuals serving in government service could during working hours take advantage of learning the other language. Once those individuals have become bilingual they should be given a preference in regard to jobs, promotions and salaries. This program should be paid for and implemented by the federal government. Many individuals will not take advantage but there should be some preference given to those who do.
It is almost impossible to take an English speaking person from Ontario and place him in a job in the northern part of the province of Quebec where the English language is not spoken. The reverse of that situation is also almost impossible. I suggest if we are going to have a bilingual country we should think in terms of true bilingualism. If this were attained we would achieve the benefits of a real bilingual culture.
One of the clauses of this bill which did not seem to create much interest is that clause having reference to political participation. Individuals in this country have a right to belong to whichever political party they desire. In countries such as England
Civil Service Act
where pride is taken regarding protection of rights of individuals there has been adopted a system of declaring certain parts of the civil service as sensitive and non-sensitive areas. I think that is a reasonable and fair system. If a similar system had been adopted by this government much of the present problem with which it is faced would have been eliminated.
The political party to which I belong is supported by membership. All citizens have the right to belong to parties so supported just as individuals have the right to belong to churches of their choice and are not penalized by other churches which do not require their members to subscribe.
We should divide our civil service into critical and non-critical or sensitive and nonsensitive areas. Individuals working in areas classed as non-sensitive would then have the right to belong and support political parties. I am not suggesting that they should be allowed to take overt political action, as a number of civil servants in Ottawa have done on occasion. I do not agree with that at all and can state that on the occasion with which I am familiar when such overt action has occurred it has not been on the part of individuals who support the party to which I belong. Many of these individuals have taken this overt action in order to get jobs in the civil service.
While discussing the bill in this particular context we should give consideration to the freedom and rights of individual citizens, whether or not they are members of the civil service. They should be allowed to participate and support any political party they choose. They should also be allowed to vote in any provincial, dominion or municipal election. There should be a clause included in this bill allowing civil servants time off in order to do that. I believe they should also be allowed under this bill to enroll in a political party if they desire. I believe that the political affiliation of civil servants has little or no effect on the jobs they have and little or no effect upon the government. I suggest, for instance, a secretary in the pool carrying a membership card of a political party causes very little concern on the part of anyone. I hope the government will give consideration to this situation.
It might be interesting to note the changes which have been made in this regard by one of our provincial legislatures. Before referring to that particular change I should like to read the "Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952", chapter 48, which is an act respecting the Civil Service of Canada.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to abuse this concession but I should like to read from that portion of the revised statutes to which I have referred, the following:
(1)	No deputy head, officer, clerk or employee in the civil service shall be debarred from voting at any dominion or provincial election if, under the laws governing said election, he has the right to vote; but no such deputy head, officer, clerk or employee shall engage in partisan work in connection with any such election or contribute, receive, or in any way deal with any money for any party funds.
(2)	Any person violating any of the provisions of this section shall be dismissed from the civil service.
Part V-Exceptions and special cases
(1)	The provisions of this act do not apply to positions in connection with the government railways or any railway owned or controlled by Her Majesty, or to any position on any ship of Her Majesty, until parliament otherwise enacts.
(2)	In this section the expression "ship of Her Majesty" includes every description of vessel, however propelled, that is used in navigation or in the improvement of navigation and is the property of or chartered or employed by Her Majesty, or the cost of which, or any portion of the cost of which has been defrayed out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.
The provisions of this act do not apply to the position of postmaster of any revenue post office the revenue of which does not exceed three thousand dollars per annum; but the preference provided by section 28, in favour of the persons mentioned therein, shall be applied in respect of appointments to such positions.
It is interesting to note that Saskatchewan in 1953 revised its statute in this regard. I should like to quote a portion of that revision. Chapter 7, part IV (i) reads as follow:
No person in the public service shall;
(a)	be in any manner compelled to take part in any political undertaking, or to make any contribution to any political party, or be in any manner threatened or discriminated against for refusing to take part in any political undertaking; or
(b)	directly or indirectly use or seek to use the authority or official influence of his position to control or modify the political action of any other person; or
(c)	during his hours of duty engage in any form of political activity; or
(d| at any time take such part in political activities as to impair his usefulness in the position in which he is employed.
(2) Any person in the public service who desires to become a candidate for public office shall be entitled to leave of absence for 30 days prior to the date of the election.
[The Deputy Chairman.]
I think we should reconsider this section and include in the federal statute some of the protections that have been adopted in Saskatchewan. This is a real threat, Mr. Chairman. Under the federal statute, people are prohibited from taking part in an active way in politics; but in Saskatchewan protection is given against making civil servants take part in electioneering in a way in which they may not wish to do. I do not wish to go into a discussion of how that sometimes happens but I should like to mention just one case. In the last provincial election in my area-I give this only by way of explanation-the civil servants who worked in the liquor control board stores, in the department of highways, and in the department of lands and forests were all given the very broad suggestion that it would be appreciated if they would spend some time in seeing that the good work being carried on by their departments was furthered by the re-election of the government candidate. At that time the premier of the province went so far as to say to some of the leading people in that riding that if the government candidate was not elected he would resign as premier of the province of Ontario. I suggest that not only should we have the protection but people should not abuse it. I am completely in agreement with this. I do not want to see government officials going around in an official capacity and speaking on behalf of the government or working for any party. I think protection should also be given against those who may be forced to do this not of their own volition. I think this particular matter should get some further consideration, Mr. Chairman. I hope the government will not be influenced by the fact that the party to which I belong has always been financed by membership fees, which are a contribution and which would probably be illegal under this legislation.

Mr. Chairman, my first words on this most important bill are to thank the Minister of Finance for his remarks last evening about the careful and intensive work done by the committee in considering the bill. I think all members who served on the committee can say with modesty that we worked many long hard hours both in committee and outside on the bill, learning of the problems of the civil service and of the administration, to bring to this house as good a bill as we possibly could.
In the course of our meetings-and there were some 23 of them-we made about 30 amendments to the bill and have brought these forward for the consideration of this committee.

I should also like to thank the hon. member tor Hull and the hon. member for Timiska-ming for their very pleasant remarks to me as chairman of the committee, in opening the debate on the bill last evening. I should like to express to them and to all members of the committee my thanks for the serious way in which they tackled the job of consideration of this civil service bill and for their co-operation at all times with me as the chairman, and with each other in the work of the committee.
I think one of the most important things about the committee, Mr. Chairman, is that it approached its task with a non-partisan attitude. All of us worked together to try to draft the best possible bill we could for the civil service and to assist the work which the civil service does for our nation.
On behalf of the committee, I should also, like to express our thanks to the civil service commissioners, the Hon. S. H. S. Hughes, Q.C., Miss Ruth Addison and Mr. Paul Pelletier, who came in day after day, and attended hour after hour, giving us so much of their time and their special knowledge and ability to assist and guide us in the work which was before us. We were also very ably assisted in very many meetings by Mr. Charles Mackenzie, the assistant secretary to the treasury board, whose advice and experience on the work of the civil service was very valuable to us in all of the months that we were working on this bill.
The briefs put forward by the civil service associations-every major civil service association in Canada brought forward briefs -were appreciated very much by the committee. The briefs were well prepared and in most instances were serious and responsible attempts to improve the working conditions of the civil service and to improve the administration of the service.
In particular I should like to compliment the members of the committee who came from the Ottawa area, the hon. members for Carleton, Hull, Ottawa East and Ottawa West, who gave considerable time and study to the bill.
While I realize that members of the committee would like to see the bill proceeded with as soon as possible, to see the improvements and advantages which flow from it made available to the civil service and to the country, I should like to take a moment to discuss a few of the improvements which will be made by the bill.
First of all, may I refer to the fact that this bill differs from the old act of 1918 in that it provides in clause 65 the right of the civil servant to his pay. This is a departure from the previous act and indeed from the general concept that the crown has no
Civil Service Act
obligation to pay any of its employees, that they receive pay as a matter of grace. As a result of this bill the civil servant has the right to go into court, come to this parliament or anywhere else to ask for his pay as of right for services rendered.
There was some commentary by the hon. member for Timiskaming and the hon. member for Hull on the widening of the powers of the deputy heads of departments. One of the purposes of the bill was to streamline the administration of the civil service and of government departments, and it was to this end that the Heeney report very strongly recommended that the powers of the deputy heads should be widened. You will note, Mr. Chairman, that coupled with the widening of the power of the deputy heads is a new provision not to be found in the old act which is there to protect the rights of the civil servant. I speak, of course, of the new appeal provisions which are to be found in the bill now before the committee. Under the old act there was no provision at all for the right of appeal except in the case of a suspension where the commission might review the situation and perhaps decide that the punishment inflicted was too severe. However, in this legislation a wide range of appeals is authorized from administrative decisions within the department and the security of the civil servant is much enhanced thereby.
A third improvement provided by this bill is in the fact that the distinction between temporary and permanent employees, which heretofore existed, has been removed. Now, even where appointments are not permanent, the employee who is in fact perhaps temporary enjoys the status and the advantages of a permanent employee of the civil service.
Another improvement which I think is noteworthy is the new clause which provides that people in the public service of Canada, in the armed forces and in the R.C.M.P., may now have the right to compete and transfer to the civil service. This was a recommendation of the Heeney report and is purposed toward the utilizing of the investment of the taxpayer in many public servants who could not otherwise follow careers in the civil service. This is an important change both for people in the R.C.M.P. and the armed forces who now have the right to transfer to the civil service and, indeed, for the people of Canada generally.
Moreover the new provision in respect of bilingualism is, I think, a very important one. When the hon. member for Hull was speaking last evening I noted that he said that he was not entirely satisfied with the provisions with regard to bilingualism. He referred to the French speaking people of Canada as poor relations. That is a phrase I have never heard

Civil Service Act
used before in speaking of the very large French speaking population of Canada and I do not think it should be accepted. He said that some preference should be provided for bilingual civil servants. The bill does in fact provide this, inasmuch as a new test has been introduced by the bill whereby when a person is to be appointed to an office he must have a knowledge of that language which is required, sufficient to serve the public of the area where he is to perform his duties. Apropos of that, Mr. Chairman, I should like to draw your attention to the comments of the Hon. S. H. S. Hughes, Q.C., chairman of the commission in speaking on this matter. He said:
Clause 47 of the bill lays upon, the commission the responsibility of seeing that this consideration-
That is the consideration that people working in an office where they will be serving both elements, French and English, should be bilingual, or in any case sufficiently so to serve the public whether French or English. I continue:
-is borne in mind not only in local positions but in head office positions of departments and not only in the language of the majority but in terms of the use of both languages where it is considered that their use is necessary to give effective service to the public. This will enable the commission in practice to give preference to applicants for positions and existing employees who are bilingual as circumstances may require.
There is in fact therefore a preference for bilingual people incorporated for the first time by the bill before the committee this afternoon.
Another change that is proposed to be made by this bill is to remove the prohibition against persons who have not been resident in Canada for five years serving in the civil service. While preference is given to Canadian citizens under the bill, where there are not persons available to fill positions within the civil service who have been in Canada for more than five years the commission can very properly turn to new Canadians who have the qualifications for the work.
I should like to turn now to what has been considered as one of the most important new provisions of the bill, and that is the construction of a new relationship between the government represented by the Minister of Finance and civil service employees. The civil service associations came before the committee asking that some form of direct consultation or negotiation should be set up between the Minister of Finance and the various staff associations so that the Department of Finance and the staff associations could gather around the table, without any intermediary, to discuss matters of pay and so on. They also suggested that some form of arbitration

should be established so that where disputes could not be settled under this new consultative process an arbitration board would be available to the parties concerned.
I am very pleased to say that at the request of these associations clause 7 of the bill was amended by the committee to provide for direct consultation between the Minister of Finance and the staff associations. It has been said that instead of using the word "consultation" the word "negotiation" should have been used. That was the position taken by the hon. member for Hull when he spoke last evening. Frankly, I see very little difference in the use of the two words. The most important thing is that clause 7 as now before the committee provides that, and I quote from clause 7:
The commission, and such member of the public service as the Minister of Finance may designate, shall from time to time consult with representatives of appropriate organizations and associations of employees with respect to pay-
And so on. In other words, the staff associations have the same right to come to the minister as the minister has to go to them to discuss pay and, through the commission, other terms and conditions. This is a very important step and I feel it meets the wishes of the great majority of the civil service in that regard.
As to the matter of arbitration, while the committee did not agree that an amendment should be made to the bill which would provide for an arbitration procedure by legislation, we are satisfied with the statements of the Minister of Finance that arbitration can be developed as it has developed in England along the lines of normal evolution.
I should point out, Mr. Chairman, that there is no need for words in the bill to establish the right of arbitration or the fact of arbitration. The bill is permissive. There is no reason why the staff associations and the Minister of Finance as parties to a dispute at any time cannot call upon an arbitration board to find a solution to their problems.
Progress reported.

Mr. Speaker, at this point I wonder whether I could give our answer to the question that was raised by the hon. member for Timiskaming, I believe about 45 minutes ago with respect to whether we might meet tonight and tomorrow evening with the intention of attempting to adjourn tomorrow

night. We are prepared to do so and we have reduced to a bare minimum the items which we think might be considered by the house before adjournment. They consist of four items, the C.N.R. financing bill, the Income Tax Act to the extent of passing second reading but not consideration of the bill in committee stage, an appropriation act, as I mentioned last night, to appropriate funds in respect of the 11 departments which have passed the committee and then interim supply to carry us on during the course of the adjournment. A fifth item might be a report from the committee on rules and procedure. As far as the government is concerned, those are the four matters that we consider could be dealt with today and tomorrow, and adjournment tomorrow night.

I regret to say that I have not any mandate to make any commitment as far as we are concerned. I am quite prepared to consult with my friends and to give an answer at six o'clock. However, I would have very grave doubts about our willingness to sit this evening. It seems to me that there are enough people having enough heart attacks around this place now without having any addition to them. I should just like to make sure that I understand correctly what the proposition is. As I understand it, the proposition is to take only the second reading of the income tax bill and the appropriation bill about which we had been given no notice until last night, I believe, something which is a very unusual procedure.

subtopic: LEGISLATION TO SAFEGUARD NAVIGATION AND FISHERIES

speakeroldname: Mr. A. D. McPhillips (Victoria, B.C.) moved
subtopic: LEGISLATION TO SAFEGUARD NAVIGATION AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-43, respecting navigation and salmon fishery on the Fraser river.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in rising to move second reading of this bill there are two things with which I wish to deal preliminarily. I have been asked why the hon. member for Victoria should be so greatly concerned about the Fraser river which, after all, is some distance from my own constituency. If the geography and habits of the Pacific salmon are understood, the reason I am concerned is readily apparent. In addition to that, I have a great many fishermen in my constituency; and I am a British Columbian and I am very proud of our Pacific salmon fishery.
Every fish caught by the fishermen who reside in my constituency is on its way to the spawning grounds of the Fraser river and its tributaries. With regard to federal jurisdiction, Mr. Speaker, some hon. members have said the Fraser river is entirely within the province of British Columbia and have asked how the parliament of Canada can have anything to do with it. There again the answer is very simple. At the time of confederation and for many years before that the Fraser river was a navigable river. Under the terms of the British North America Act the parliament of Canada has control over rivers that were navigable rivers at the time of confederation. Also, the parliament of Canada has control over the deep-sea fisheries off our coasts and the attendant inland fisheries which result from those deep-sea fisheries. Therefore on two counts the parliament of Canada has every right to deal with the Fraser river and what goes on in the Fraser river, both from the standpoint of navigation and fisheries.
The average value of the Pacific salmon industry is approximately $90 million per annum. In 1962, when there will be the great Adams river run again-Adams river is a tributary of the Fraser river-the industry will be worth a great deal more; but it averages $90 million. This is to say nothing of the huge investment in fishing vessels, nets, equipment and all the money paid out 90205-6-487
Private Bills
in wages for building those ships, nets, equipment and paying all the people employed in the fishery.
There is something else, Mr. Speaker, that I think this house should know if it does not know it already. The Fraser river of British Columbia is the greatest salmon river in the world. Prior to the industry on the Fraser river there had been a salmon fishery on the Columbia river in the United States, on the coast of Oregon and in the upper regions of that river. It was not as large an industry as ours; it was not nearly so valuable, but it was valuable earlier. The Fraser river fishery was developed and the techniques existing on the Columbia river were followed.
I know that when I was a boy the term "Columbia river boat" was commonly used. This was the type of boat that nearly all our gillnetters used and was a boat that had been developed in connection with that fishery on the Columbia river. It is common knowledge that the fishery on the Columbia is ruined. It is true that a few fish spawn in the Priest river, one of its tributaries. However to all intents and purposes the great fishery on that river is ruined. It was ruined because of the construction, at the time of the late President Roosevelt and his new deal, of two new dams on that river, the Bonneville dam close to the mouth of the Columbia and the huge Grand Coulee dam which is very much further up the river.
At that time the president of the United States was worried about it, and I will deal with that later. But we had a procession of professors and engineers who assured the president of the United States, "There is nothing to this. Salmon and dams can exist on the Columbia river". I have every respect, and always have had, for professors and engineers, but when it comes to a spawning river I have a lot more respect for the Pacific salmon.
In the case of Bonneville, because of the treaty signed many years ago between Canada and the United States, the United States agreed that they would not interfere with navigation on the Columbia river and a ship canal and lock were built on the Bonneville dam. Would you believe, Mr. Speaker, that some of the professors and engineers said, "Well, that is how the salmon will get up. When the canal gates are open to let a ship in, the salmon will swim in with it; and when it is taken up, the salmon will swim out"? They did not know much about the Pacific salmon, because that certainly did not happen.
I have a work here which is really the only work on this subject in the form in which it is written. It is a book written about the Columbia river fishery by Anthony Netboy

Private Bills
entitled "Salmon of the Pacific northwest. Fish v. dams". I am indebted to the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee) for bringing this work to my attention. In effect this book is an apologia, because Netboy was one of the men who thought this thing could be accomplished on the Columbia river and he afterwards wrote a sort of apologia. At page 10 of the foreword-which was written by the late Senator Neuberger of the state of Oregon, who was a great proponent of the maintenance of the fishery in that river -there is found this passage:
"Go and investigate the fish v. dams question," Mr. Netboy was told by Henry Alderman, then the assistant to Dr. Paul J. Raver, Bonneville's administrator.
So Mr. Netboy did go and make some investigations, but regrettably he came up with the wrong report and is now apologizing for it. At page 42 of this work, under the heading "Enter the federal dams", there are a few excerpts which I should like to read:
The diminishing runs of salmon, resulting from numerous and complex causes, had long worried the fishery industry when a new and potentially adverse factor entered the picture-start of construction in 1933 on Bonneville dam, followed shortly by ground-breaking for mammoth Grand Coulee dam. Bonneville was located on the Columbia 145 miles from its mouth, Grand Coulee 597 miles from Astoria.
That is a city at the mouth of the Columbia.
Bonneville was to have a 60-foot head, Grand Coulee 316 feet. Never before had a major salmon run been required to hurdle an obstruction as formidable as Bonneville.
The first barriers constructed in the Columbia river watershed were primarily irrigation dams. They were not the massive structures that came into being with the development of the river's hydroelectric potential. Some of the earlier dams built on the tributaries for power and irrigation diversions did not include facilities for passing fish migrating upstream. Consequently, a terrific toll was exacted at these points on certain races of Columbia river salmon. In fact, entire runs into several tributaries were almost completely wiped out.
In addition to dams without fish passage facilities, many other dams were built in the Columbia river basin that had provisions for passage of adult fish, such as the low dam at Willamette falls (Oregon City). But even here no safe passage was provided to the downstream migrants-the tiny fish.
That is the fingerlings that have to come down:
When the Bonneville project was authorized by President Roosevelt as a public works project, Frank Bell, U.S. commissioner of fisheries, was requested to find some way of getting the salmon over the dam. "I wrote to every civilized country in the world," said Mr. Bell, and "at no place... could we find where they had passed fish over as high a dam as Bonneville would be."
Naturally there were widespread-almost hysterical-fears that Bonneville would spell the end of the Columbia river salmon runs and confine the fishery to the lower river, thus wiping out part of an industry then valued at some $10 million

annually. In an article in the Saturday Evening Post in November, 1937, when the dam was nearing completion, Richard L. Neuberger wrote:
That is the late senator I mentioned before.
"Prevalent throughout the principal salmon-producing region of the world today is the almost unshakable opinion that within a few years the fighting fish with the flaky flesh will be one and the same with the dodo bird-extinct". Not only were commercial fishermen, anglers, and the salmon industry generally apprehensive, but scientists and conservationists from distant parts of the country felt obliged to voice their fears. For example, Arthur Newton Pack, president of the American nature association, declared that the dams being built on the Columbia would kill a fishing industry providing employment to more than 25,000 people annually. E. D. Clark, secretary of the association of Pacific fisheries, claimed that the dams would be disastrous. He foresaw the end of the runs of the giant Chinook.
The Indians were equally pessimistic. According to Neuberger, George Red Hawk, aged chief of the Cayuse Indians, who was spearing salmon on the river before the railroads had even reached the Columbia gorge, "looked grimly at the surging river. 'White man's dams,' he said, 'mean no more salmon.' "
Such strenuous objections were raised by fishery people to the blockading of the river by Bonneville dam that the corps of engineers was forced to include fish passage facilities in the plans for this structure. At first they were to consist of only four conventional ladders of moderate size-like those at Oregon City-estimated to cost $800,000. When fishery biologists demonstrated that they would be palpably inadequate to handle the large fish traffic using this stretch of the river, an elaborate system of traps, locks, elevators, canals and ladders was devised which added $7 million to the cost of the dam.
Notwithstanding that expenditure the Columbia river fishery has been ruined and that great source of food no longer exists. That, as I say, appears in this author's book, which is an apologia for his previous advice which he now admits was faulty.
Today in British Columbia we have engineers coming up again with the same sort of applesauce as they fed to President Roosevelt. I have an example right here. This is from the Canadian Press of June, 1961 under a Vancouver dateline. It appeared in just about all the papers in British Columbia and, I think, throughout Canada generally. The heading is: "Both Power Systems and Fish Possible in B.C. River System" and the article reads:
British Columbia can have both fish and power from its fast-flowing river systems, the engineering institute of Canada was told today.
Papers presented at the institute's annual meeting indicated that the baffling problem of building power dams and at the same time allowing salmon to get to their spawning grounds, has at last reached a stage of solution.
The papers indicated, too, that with proper measures the salmon yield can be substantially increased. At the same time, continued and increased research was urged.
Val Gwyther, Vancouver consulting engineer, stated:

"The present policy of retardation of power development in a watershed, due to our inability to produce the answer to beneficial fish migration, is in the past, and these watersheds now are open in development of both fish and power."
There is no doubt, Mr. Gwyther said, that we now can produce salmon species in great quantities, jointly with other resource values, and with economy.
Mr. Gwyther's paper went at length into the problems of fish propagation. Rearing capacities of natural and impounded lakes should be utilized by artificial fertilization and incubation of eggs to give a yield far in excess of that from natural spawning grounds.
There again, all we have is a pious statement from this engineer that everything is now all right. But you never see any concrete statement as to how it is going to be done. What bothers me at the present time, because of the difficulty existing in British Columbia, because of the attitude of that government in British Columbia, the trouble with the Columbia and the Peace river, is this: I am fearful that we are going to wake up one day and find that the premier of British Columbia has given a water licence on the Fraser river. The British Columbia Electric Company is ready now and has been ready for years. They have all the plans ready. They can jump on the Fraser tomorrow and build two dams. That is what faces us, and that is why I think, now, that the parliament of Canada has a right to put an end to this thing forever and keep this great source of food, this great river and the industry which depends on it safe for Canadians now and forever. We should do that now before we lose it. I bespeak the support of hon. members for the passage of this bill.
