subtopic: LEGISLATION TO SAFEGUARD NAVIGATION AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
I just wanted to make sure that I was referring to the right bill. As the seconder of the bill sponsored by the hon. member for Victoria I thought perhaps I should indicate what my interest is in this matter.
My constituency, and particularly the Richmond portion of it is situated at the mouth of the Fraser river. It should also be obvious to all hon. members present that I am interested in this particular measure because of the existence of the community of Steveston, which is a fishing community located very close to the mouth of the Fraser. At the peak of the fishing season approximately 10,000 fishermen actually base their salmon fishing activities in that area.
First, I felt I should point out that although I am the seconder of this bill and approve of the principles enunciated therein, I do not think it goes far enough. When I spoke earlier in respect of this bill, actually in 1959, I said at that time that although I endorsed the principles I felt that the bill did not perhaps go as far as I should have liked.
In the first part of the bill the sponsor has drawn attention to the fact that there should not be any hydroelectric power dams or other navigation dams which would obstruct salmon fishing. However, in the second part of the bill it is suggested that this would not apply to any project of the government of Canada dealing with navigation, flood control, river bed erosion, current control and so on.
During one of the meetings of the fisheries committee the sensitivity of this salmon fishery was very forcefully drawn to our attention. The only point that concerns me about the hon. member's bill is that the government of Canada, despite how well meaning it is, may nevertheless create the very difficulties which the sponsor of this bill is attempting to obviate.
The second report of the fisheries committee of 1959 at page 85 states as follows:
Your committee held seven meetings, one of which was devoted to the consideration of a preliminary report on flood control and hydroelectric
Private Bills
power in the Fraser river basin in British Columbia, particularly in respect of fisheries and certain relevant aspects referred to in the said report.
This report then states:
Your committee recommends that the government consider the advisability of hastening the re-appointment of the Fraser river board in conjunction with the government of British Columbia in order that the said board achieve its aims, specially with reference to the protection of fisheries in all its aspects.
The committee went on to make this further important recommendation unanimously:
Your committee expresses the opinion that no dams should be built on the Fraser river, or any of its tributaries, where such dams will, in the opinion of the Minister of Fisheries, interfere with, or be detrimental to anadromous fish runs.
I think the very important point raised there is that the control and supervision should be in the hands of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean) and his departmental officials because it seems to me that there is a patent loophole in the second part of this bill which would make it possible for irreparable damage to be done to these particular fish runs.
I think that the sponsor of this bill indicated the legislative justification for the amendments contained in this bill when he drew attention to the fact that it came within the British North America Act. This particular phase of the situation does specifically come within section 91 (2) of that act which deals with coastal and inland fisheries. The matter of jurisdiction in this regard is recorded in the Canada Year Book for 1960 at page 630. I should like to read a portion of what is stated there, as follows:
The British North America Act gave the federal government full legislative jurisdiction for the coastal and inland fisheries of Canada and under this act laws are made for the protection, conservation and development of the fisheries throughout the country. However, the provinces have, by agreement, assumed administrative responsibilities in varying degrees. Consequently, though all the regulations governing fishing are made by the federal government, the work of administering the fisheries (enforcing the different laws and regulations, inspecting fish products, issuing licences, etc.) is done without duplication of staff either by federal or by provincial officers, according to arrangements.
That is further supported by the contention that the Minister of Fisheries and his department must have very strong supervision, which is referred to at page 631 of the Canada Year Book. The responsibilities of the Department of Fisheries are set out very succinctly there. I should like to quote a paragraph which deals with these responsibilities, as follows:
The chief responsibilities of the Department of Fisheries throughout Canada are, in brief: to conserve and develop Canada's primary fishery resources: to encourage the development of the

Private Bills
fishing industry in the national economy; to inspect fish products, establish standards of quality and promote the optimum utilization of the resource; and to develop a proper public understanding of the resource and the industry.
We had indications during the hearings of the fisheries committee that the value of the fishing industry on the Fraser river was some $34,500,000. This is a very important industry and every effort should be made to maintain it properly. I believe the fact that we have two other great rivers in British Columbia- the Columbia which has a potential of some 3 million horsepower and the Peace which has a potential of some 4 million horsepower -should warrant the protection of salmon fishing on the Fraser. The enactment of legislation such as is before us now would force individuals in British Columbia who are interested in developing power, first of all, into using the potentialities of those two rivers. I would suggest that by that time we would possibly not require any further development or utilization of a river such as the Fraser. We have seen the tremendous developments that have gone on in atomic research. At the recent hearings of the research committee it was drawn to our attention that they expect very soon to have the CANDU power unit installed at Rolphton which will be producing some 200,000 kilowatts. First of all I think we should exhaust those rivers, the Columbia and the Peace, and then see what progress is being made on atomic power. At that time it might be possible to take a further look at the Fraser river.
During the proceedings of the committee in 1959, in dealing with this matter of research and what can be done, I was interested in the statements we had from Dr. Pritchard. On questioning him I was particularly interested to find out whether it would be possible to hurry up the process by concentrating perhaps more scientists on this particular problem. He indicated to me that there was in total in the neighbourhood of some 75 scientists and engineers working on the problem and they are spending approximately $3 million on research alone. I think it is fair to say that despite all the engineers, biologists and so forth working on this particular project there had been developed to date no clear-cut and adequate solution to the problem of getting the fish up over the dam and then getting them downstream safely. That, of course, is simplifying the problem.
There have been some statements and arguments that the fisheries people in British Columbia are opposed to the development of hydroelectric power. I think it would be
[Mr. Drysdale.l
only fair, Mr. Speaker, to reiterate the remarks in the brief that was put out by the fisheries association of British Columbia, dated February 1, 1958. On page 2 of this brief we find the following;
The fisheries association of British Columbia takes this opportunity of stating unequivocally that it is not opposed to the development of hydro power but rather believes that the sources of electricity should and can be developed under careful and judicious planning so that the runs of fish in the salmon bearing rivers will not be obstructed or otherwise harmed. If it could be shown conclusively by the fishery engineers and biologists that those biological problems which will result from the development of hydro sites on fish bearing rivers could be overcome with certainty then, and only then, would we have no objection to the construction of power dams on such rivers. Today, the best advice available from the fishery biologists is that the construction of dams on the diversion of rivers into salmon bearing rivers will create consequential physical and biological problems which will destroy the fish.
In this same brief they go on to make several specific recommendations which I think might be of interest to hon. members. At page 4 they say:
In order to ensure that there will be an ever increasing supply of power available to the industrial and domestic consumers in the province of British Columbia, it would appear advisable that the responsible public authorities should ensure that the following steps be taken to utilize all the natural resources of this country in an orderly, considered program of development:
(a)	The development of hydro sites on non-fish bearing streams should receive the first attention of those parties engaged in the production and distribution of electricity. In addition, the public utility companies should ensure that presently developed sites are brought up to maximum production.
(b)	The fact that western Canada is endowed with a great wealth of gas, petroleum and coal, thus ensuring an alternate source of energy for the production of power, should be recognized and such alternate sources of energy should be utilized to the fullest in conjunction with the development of hydro sites as previously mentioned.
(c)	A responsible agency should cause a provincewide power grid system to be developed with connections to Alberta and the United States, the purpose of this grid system being to enable a local region having a surplus of power, and such a situation exists today, to conveniently transmit such surplus to another region having a shortage. This exchange of surplus power back and forth would ensure that those hydro and thermal sources already developed would be utilized to their fullest advantage.
We believe that if these complementary steps are taken we will find nuclear and atomic sources of power available and feasible in time to meet growing needs for power and avoid destruction of the fishery resource.
I think it is particularly timely that the hon. member has brought up his bill at this moment. Because of the many discussions of power sites in British Columbia, I think the bill, if it should pass, would do an exceedingly great service to British Columbia by serving

to concentrate power development on the nonsalmon bearing streams, thus ensuring that the fish runs of the Fraser river will be maintained through perpetuity.

subtopic: LEGISLATION TO SAFEGUARD NAVIGATION AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure not many members of the house will find themselves in disagreement with the principle of this bill which is that nothing should be done by way of placing obstructions in the Fraser that shall damage this great food source. In view of the ever increasing world population and the shortage of food it becomes more important with the passage of time. I think also we should not look at it entirely from the point of view of the value that is there at the present time because this is not only a renewable resource but one which can be vastly increased. A fairly intensive study has been made of this subject by the Fraser river board which was set up for the purpose of studying flood control and hydroelectric power in the Fraser river basin. I should like to refer to two or three statements in that report. At page 142, in dealing with the value of the fishery on the Fraser river-and I think perhaps it may be of interest to the house to have on record something of the value of the British Columbia fishery as a whole and the position of the Fraser river in relation to it-we find the following:
In addition to the fish taken by Canadian fishermen there was a catch by United States fishermen of salmon of British Columbia origin which at 1957 prices had an average annual value of $15,525,000, of which $13,651,000 was of fish originating in the Fraser river. Therefore, the average annual value of the salmon catch originating in British Columbia waters (1952-55) at 1957 prices was $68,665,000, of which the Fraser river contributed $34,574,000, or 50.3 per cent.
That is, 50.3 per cent of the total fish production of British Columbia. To go over something of the history of the Fraser river it should be noted that it is only in very recent years that we have got anywhere near the potential of the river, because back in 1913 during the construction of the transcontinental railroad, there was a blockage of the stream which to a large extent prevented the fish from getting up to spawn. It is only in very recent years indeed that we have made a little headway in overcoming that problem. The report to which I referred previously reported on that matter as follows:
The rock obstruction in the Fraser canyon at Hells Gate caused by the construction of a transcontinental railroad in 1913 resulted in a serious blockage to the passage of salmon at certain water levels which decimated the early migrating sockeye runs to the Chilko, Quesnel, Stuart and Nechako systems in subsequent years. The pink salmon run in 1913 was also seriously affected by the obstruction-
Private Bills
The paragraph goes on in that vein. I simply draw it to the attention of the house to show what any obstruction in this river can do to the runs of salmon. In 1945 and 1946 this was partially corrected by fishways which were constructed at Hells Gate where the river had been blocked. The board had the following statement to make in regard to it:
Since 1946 the commission has been responsible for regulating the commercial fishery for sockeye so as to obtain adequate escapement consistent with the commission's objectives and at the same time divide the allowable catch equally between fishermen of both nations. After removing the obstructions, scientific principles were applied to managing the fishery, the results of which have been outstanding. In two cycles following the completion of the Hells Gate fishways the commercial catch of sockeye increased from 6,478,000 in the period 1947-50 to 18,246,000 in the period 1951-54.
I am sure the house will appreciate the record increase that took place in the production of fish from that river after the obstruction was removed. The report goes on to state further:
It is expected that the total cyclic catch can be increased to at least 46 million fish when all the runs are fully rehabilitated.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, these runs cannot be rehabilitated if there are going to be obstructions placed in the Fraser river. For that reason I am fully in accord with the bill. I wish to refer to the report made by the fisheries committee in 1959, which has already been referred to by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond, because I think that the suggestion made by the committee might have been taken into consideration in the bill. The report reads in part as follows:
Your committee expresses the opinion that no dams should be built on the Fraser river, or any of its tributaries, where such dams will, in the opinion of the Minister of Fisheries, interfere with, or be detrimental to anadromous fish runs.
I think that provision might well have been incorporated in the bill. That could be done, of course, if the bill were referred to a committee for study. However, whether or not that provision is added I certainly am fully in support of the bill and I would recommend it to the house.

subtopic: LEGISLATION TO SAFEGUARD NAVIGATION AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not believe that previous speakers have pointed out the fact that the Fraser river, one of the three great rivers in the province of British Columbia, the other two being the Columbia and the Peace, is the only one of the three that is completely within the province of British Columbia. One feature of the bill that has not been mentioned is the diking or flood control of the river.

Business of the House
As I see the situation, there are three problems, the protection of the salmon, prospective power use and the control of flooding, the last problem being connected in every way with the other two. Hon. members will recall that in the 1948 and 1950 floods very great damage was done in the lower Fraser valley. When I refer to the lower Fraser valley I mean the area from Hope to Vancouver or to the coast, a distance of 100 miles.
After the flood of 1948 work was immediately started to put the dikes into proper shape and it was considered as being completed in 1950. Since then, however, the dikes have been eroded. The current has cut under some of them and at the moment the people of the Fraser valley are very much concerned about what will happen during the next flood.
The boards of trade of Hope, Chilliwack, Agassiz, Mission and Abbotsford are all concerned about this matter and these boards are all represented in the associated boards of trade of the Fraser valley. A great deal of damage was done in that year and the boards of trade, as do many of the residents, feel that now is the time to put these dikes into proper shape. If the dikes go out the Fraser will run rampant and do damage again.
Hon. members may not know that every year there are two dredges working all the time between the mouth of the Chilliwack river where it empties into the Fraser about 12 miles west of Chilliwack and the town of Hope. These dredges work continually year in and year out which is an indication of how much damage is done by rubbish, trees, stumps, sand bars, gravel bars and so on in the river. The river has to be kept open for the transportation of logs from Hope right to the coast. Several companies are involved in this business and it is a great industry in the Fraser valley.
The Fraser river flood control report has suggested dams in places where they will not interfere with the salmon. I believe that the one location that is most suitable for flood control is at Clearwater north of Kamloops on the Thompson river. Apparently this would not damage the Ash in any way.

speechtext: May I inquire what the business will be for tomorrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I made a suggestion at five o'clock, Mr. Speaker, with regard to the business of the house. I suggested then that in

the view of the government we would like to adjourn tomorrow some time, perhaps tomorrow night, if the house sees fit. We have reduced to a bare minimum the items which we feel should be considered before an adjournment should take place. In answer to the hon. member for Timiskaming, I also said that we on this side were prepared to sit tonight.
With these propositions before the house, the order of business for tomorrow would be as follows: The C.N.R. bill, which it is necessary to complete, the Income Tax Act, which would be carried to the completion of second reading but would not be considered in the committee stage, an appropriation bill for the supply which has already passed through the committee, and interim supply. I said that there might also be a report from the procedure committee, which has been sitting under the chairmanship of Mr. Speaker, dealing with certain matters pertaining to divorce. I should like an expression of opinion from the other side of the house with respect to whether that report might be tabled and considered tomorrow or whether under the circumstances non-contentious divorce bills would be considered and passed by the house tomorrow.
I put three propositions before the house for consideration: First, whether or not we should sit tonight; second, whether on the basis of attempting adjournment tomorrow night we might consider the four items of business I have outlined and, third, whether or not the divorce bills should be considered and the non-contentious ones passed or whether the report of the rules committee on that matter should be brought before the house for consideration.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the second suggestion should be taken first. In so far as that is concerned, I think we would have to say to the house leader that I do not see how it would be possible for the other place to deal with the three matters that are now before us and to complete them by Saturday night if they sat until twelve o'clock. I understood His Honour, the Speaker, to say that the Senate had adjourned until three o'clock tomorrow afternoon. That would leave a very short time in which to deal with (1) the Senate amendments, (2) the industrial development bank bill, and (3) the Coyne matter-
And the C.N.R. bill.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
-and other matters such as the C.N.R. bill and the bills that would go through the house tomorrow. It is therefore rather difficult for those of us who sit on this side of the chamber to see how they could dispose of those important items of legislation in such a short time. I think

that deals with the second item, namely the matter of sitting tonight. I do not think we could give consent to sit tonight.
So far as the non-contentious divorce matters are concerned, I presume that matter would be taken up tomorrow and I would rather rely on the opinion of my friend the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate on matters of divorce than give my own opinion on it. But in so far as the items mentioned by the house leader are concerned, namely the C.N.R. bill and the bill to amend the Income Tax Act, may I say that I can see no reason why we could not deal with those tomorrow. However, I should like to get an explanation of two other matters, namely why it is thought necessary to bring in an appropriation act. It has been the custom to bring in an appropriation act when all the estimates have been disposed of, but not when only a portion of the estimates have been disposed of as is the case at the present time.
Finally, in so far as interim supply is concerned, can the house leader indicate how much would be required?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have just one or two comments to make. As to the activities of the other place, may I say that I am not entirely familiar with their course of procedure. However, I assume that their adjournment which was reported to us this afternoon was based on an understanding of the business which would be coming before them, and I reached the conclusion that they had considered that they would have sufficient time tomorrow in which to deal with these matters. They have no automatic adjournment and can sit just as long as they wish to sit.
The two questions with regard to the appropriation act and interim supply could more appropriately be answered by the Minister of Finance. As I understand it, the appropriation bill is simply to deal with supply which has already been approved by the house for 11 departments. They have gone through committee. The total amount of money there would be summed up in an appropriation bill and would be voted. As to interim supply- and there again the Minister of Finance would be able to give the answer to that question- may I say this. It has been normal for us to ask for two months' supply at a time. Perhaps the house might consider it to be wiser to grant it for a longer period than that. I do not know; it would be up to the house to determine that matter.

If I might accept the suggestion of the hon. member for Laurier that I should make a reference to this matter of divorce, may I say this. It is a well known fact that in our party we regard this matter 90205-6-488
Business of the House
as one of individual conscience. Any proposition that may be put before the house I am sure will be treated respectfully in that way. I think perhaps I need say no more about that matter.
I have had a word with my hon. friend, while the house leader was speaking, about the proposed appropriation bill. This is an unprecedented suggestion or, while there may be some precedent somewhere, it is certainly an unusual suggestion. I suggest to the government that they should not proceed with this idea for this reason. This appropriation bill will preclude any possibility on the part of the opposition of raising on a subsequent appropriation bill any of the matters connected with all those departments of government where supply has been voted. It seems to me that, after all, the most sacred of all our rights in the opposition is the right of airing grievances before we grant supply. The government will be in no better position after having passed this bill than they were before it was passed. They will have interim supply to last them until such time as we come back. We would feel that the more urgent business of the country should be given priority over a measure of this sort that does not seem to serve any purpose whatsoever. As for the interim supply, when the Minister of Finance indicates what his desires are in that matter I am sure my friend the Leader of the Opposition will be prepared to give his views on the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: With regard to the appropriation bill may I say this. I will take into consideration with my colleagues the suggestion made from the other side. It may be possible to meet their wishes in that regard. May we hear from the C.C.F. with regard to these proposals or certainly with regard to the divorce bills?

I think the thoughts of the C.C.F. were expressed by the hon. member for Timiskaming with regard to sitting this evening and looking towards recessing or adjourning tomorrow. That possibility of sitting in the evening does not exist now.
As to the question of divorce, this is a latter reference of the minister and I understand it involves a report of a committee under your chairmanship, Mr. Speaker. I think it would be unwise now to make any comment on the contents of that report, as it has not yet been presented to the house. Perhaps this is something we can approach tomorrow.
It being 10 minutes after six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
